summary: Defines Sensor Measurement Lists, a simple data model for reporting sensor measurements and device parameters. It has representations in JSON, CBOR, XML and EXI. A record can carry things like a name, unit, value and time, so small devices and the systems reading them can exchange readings in a common form.

eli5.summary: Many thermometers and gadgets each write their numbers in their own style. This gives them one shared way to write down a reading so everyone can read it.

questions: what do the senml fields bn and bt mean
subtitle: A small, common format for sensor readings and device settings, in JSON, CBOR, XML and EXI.

tldr.problem: Simple, constrained devices need to send measurements in small packets, and servers need to collect many of them efficiently, without each vendor inventing its own format.
tldr.mechanism: SenML defines one data model, an array of Records with short labels such as n, u, v and t. Base fields like a Base Name or Base Time apply to later Records so they need not be repeated. The model has JSON, CBOR, XML and EXI representations.
tldr.outcome: A sensor can report with a few labelled fields, and the same model can also carry configuration and actuation requests. RFC 8428 has since been updated by RFC 9100.

facts.label: Implementation target
facts.value: roughly 1 KB of flash on an 8-bit microprocessor

today: RFC 8428 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9100, so read the two together.

sections.title: What SenML Is For
sections.content:
Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML) is a format and a set of media types for carrying simple sensor information in protocols such as HTTP and CoAP. It is meant so that very limited processors can easily encode a measurement, while a server can still collect a large number of them efficiently. It supports sensors pushing data feeds to a collector, and the web model where a client requests the data as a resource, for example GET /sensor/temperature.

SenML strikes a balance. The data is self-describing, carrying some information about the sensor, but the extra information is kept to a fairly minimal set for efficiency. Other information can be found by other means, such as the CoRE Link Format. The RFC says plainly that many more complex kinds of measurement are not a good fit.

The data is a single array of SenML Records. A Record can have fields such as a sensor identifier, the time of the measurement, the unit and the current value. Here is the RFC's first example:

[
  {"n":"urn:dev:ow:10e2073a01080063","u":"Cel","v":23.1}
]

This is one Record for a sensor with the given name, reporting a current value of 23.1 degrees Celsius.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny form for a sensor to fill in: which sensor I am, what I measured, in what unit and when. A collector can then read forms from thousands of sensors the same way.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The goal is to send simple measurements in small packets from large numbers of constrained devices, including over networks such as 6LoWPAN. The authors say there is a desire to implement it in roughly 1 KB of flash on an 8-bit microprocessor.

Experience with power meters and other large deployments showed that several measurements need to fit in a single HTTP or CoAP request. This batch upload helps servers support many devices, and helps proxies and storage devices even when a sensor sends one item at a time.

To keep messages small, the Name need not be repeated in every Record. A Base Name is prepended to the Name of its Record and of the Records after it. Time can be absolute or relative, since some devices have accurate time and others do not. A sensor with no wall-clock time might take a measurement every second, batch up 60, and send them with times relative to when the batch was sent. A server with accurate time can then convert them to absolute times.
sections.eli5: Tiny gadgets cannot afford long messages. So the form lets you write the sensor's name once at the top and just list the numbers underneath, and lets a gadget say 'five seconds ago' if it has no clock.

sections.title: Records, Base Fields and Labels
sections.content:
A SenML Pack is one array of SenML Records. Each Record can hold two kinds of fields. Base fields apply to that Record and to all Records after it, up to but not including the next Record that has the same base field. Regular fields apply to that Record only. All base fields are optional.

The base fields are Base Name (bn), Base Time (bt), Base Unit (bu), Base Value (bv), Base Sum (bs) and Base Version (bver, a positive integer that defaults to 10). The regular fields are Name (n), Unit (u), the value fields, Sum (s), Time (t) and Update Time (ut).

There are four kinds of value: a floating-point number (v), a boolean (vb), a string (vs) and binary data (vd). Exactly one value field MUST appear unless there is a Sum field. The Name, once appended to the Base Name, must give a globally unique identifier. That concatenated name MUST use only letters, digits and the characters hyphen, colon, period, slash and underscore, and MUST start with a letter or digit. URIs or URNs are RECOMMENDED.

A Record is resolved when it has no base values (except Base Version) and no relative times; resolving applies the Pack's base values to it. Resolved form is useful for big data applications and when converting to other formats.
sections.eli5: Imagine a list where the first line says 'all of these are from the kitchen thermometer, in degrees'. Every later line only needs the number. Resolving the list means writing the shared words onto every line.

sections.title: Time, Values and Sums
sections.content:
The Base Time and Time are added together to get the time of the measurement; a missing one counts as zero. The Base Value and Value are added the same way, and so are the Base Sum and Sum. A Record with no Unit uses the Base Unit.

Time is a number of seconds. Values less than 268,435,456 (2 to the power 28) are relative to "now". A time of zero means the sensor does not know the absolute time and the measurement was made roughly now, a negative value is seconds in the past, and a positive value is seconds in the future, which is useful for actuation. Values greater than or equal to 268,435,456 are absolute times relative to the Unix epoch. Care is needed so that the sum of Base Time and Time does not accidentally reach 268,435,456 when a relative time was intended.

The Sum field is the integrated sum of the values over time, in the Unit multiplied by seconds. For something like an electrical meter, the cumulative total is less error-prone than summing per-second power readings, and it still reflects what happened while the network was down. The RFC warns that sums are loosely defined: they may wrap to zero, may reset when the device is reset or replaced, and the start of accumulation is unknown. Sum is not suitable for event counts or interface byte counters, which can go straight into the Value field.

SenML can also configure parameters and drive actuators. A Pack sent to a target that treats it as configuration is read as a request to set the named resources to the given values at the given times.
sections.eli5: A reading can say 'right now', 'five seconds ago', or give a real clock time. A running total, like a meter that only counts up, is handy because even if you miss some reports, the total still shows how much happened.

sections.title: JSON, CBOR, XML and EXI
sections.content:
The JSON form (application/senml+json) is an array with one JSON object per Record, using the labels as member names. Only UTF-8 is allowed. Data values are base64 encoded with the URL-safe alphabet and padding omitted. Receivers MUST handle the range of IEEE double-precision numbers, and an exponent's e MUST be lower case.

The CBOR form (application/senml+cbor) is equivalent to JSON, but uses integers as labels for compactness: base values get negative labels (for example bn is -2) and the others get non-negative ones (for example n is 0 and v is 2). Streaming uses an indefinite-length array; non-streaming SenML MUST use a definite length.

The XML form (application/senml+xml) puts each Record in a senml element inside a sensml element, with the fields as attributes. The EXI form (application/senml-exi) is a binary encoding of that XML. It SHOULD use the strict schema mode, which drops extensions. The EXI header MUST include EXI Options with a schemaId of a.

For one example of 13 Records, the RFC reports that JSON takes 573 and XML 649, while CBOR takes 254 and EXI 161. After gzip the gap narrows.
sections.eli5: The same form can be written in four languages: plain readable text, a compact number code, a tag-based text, and a squeezed-down binary. The facts are the same in all four, only the size differs.

sections.title: Extensions, Streams and Fragments
sections.content:
SenML can be extended with new custom base or regular fields. Implementations MUST ignore fields they do not recognise, unless the label name ends with _, in which case an error MUST be generated. All Records in a Pack MUST have the same version, and a reader MUST NOT use an object whose Base Version is larger than it understands.

Streaming has its own media types. A Sensor Streaming Measurement List (SenSML) is sent and read piece by piece, so a Record can be used as soon as it arrives. Relative times in a stream are measured from when that Record is sent. Using SenML in this way is optional, but a protocol that does so MUST say so.

A fragment identifier can pick Records out of a Pack with the rec scheme, counting from 1. For example coap://example.com/temp#rec=3-6 selects the 3rd to 6th Records, and 19-* means the 19th to the last. A selected Record still has to be read in the context of the Pack's base values. Static metadata about devices is not carried in SenML, and can be provided out of band, for example with the CoRE Link Format.
sections.eli5: You can add your own extra boxes to the form, but the reader must either ignore a box it does not know or, if the box name ends in an underscore, refuse to continue. You can also point at line 3 to 6 of a long list.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Sensor data ranges from very public, like outdoor temperature, to very private, such as patient health information. When SenML is used for configuration or actuation, it can change the state of systems and the physical world, for example by turning off a heater or opening a lock. The RFC warns that malicious use could have severe consequences, potentially including loss of life.

The SenML formats provide no security themselves and rely on the carrying protocol, such as HTTP with TLS or S/MIME, for confidentiality, integrity and authentication. The formats contain no executable content, though future extensions could add some. Because Records are interpreted with their base values, a Record separated from the one that sets the base values becomes useless or wrong, so the integrity of unresolved Packs matters.

The privacy section adds that long-term stable unique identifiers in Names can be a privacy problem, and should be used with care or avoided.
sections.eli5: The form does not lock the envelope. It depends on the courier carrying it to do that. Be extra careful when the form is used to tell a device to do something, like unlock a door.
